messages.content: Analyze this sentence.  "Consydre thou myne condicyon; reflecte upon myne fader. Shall I forsake hym, when he is strycken wyth blyndnesse and destytute, to wrastle wyth infirmitie and penurye, when it lyeth wythin my poure to rendre hys latter yeeres fylled wyth comforte and joye?" Each paragraph of your response must end with the same word it started with, separate paragraphs with a newline.

message.content:
Archaic diction and spelling appear in condicyon, fader, strycken, blyndnesse, destytute, infirmitie, penurye, poure, yeeres, fylled, comforte, and joye, marking the line as early modern or imitated early modern English. Archaic
Grammatically the sentence opens with the imperative Consydre thou myne condicyon, continues with the imperative reflecte upon myne fader, and then poses the rhetorical question Shall I forsake hym, with subordinate clauses describing the father's blindness, destitution, infirmity, and poverty. Grammatically
Ethically the passage argues against forsaking a helpless father, because the speaker has the power, poure, to make the father's latter years filled with comforte and joye rather than infirmitie and penurye. Ethically
